clinicalPearls: An inherited haemolytic anaemia caused by defects in red cell membrane structural proteins, producing rigid, spherical red cells that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen
The classic triad is anaemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly, with severity ranging from an incidental finding to transfusion-dependent disease
Most cases follow autosomal dominant inheritance, and a positive family history is common, though sporadic mutations also occur
The blood film shows spherocytes lacking central pallor, with a raised reticulocyte count and increased mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration
Chronic haemolysis predisposes to pigment (bilirubin) gallstones and to neonatal jaundice; folate demands are increased
Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 infection can cause an abrupt, dangerous fall in haemoglobin by shutting down red cell production

Diagnosis is supported by a negative direct antiglobulin test (distinguishing it from autoimmune haemolysis) together with confirmatory tests such as the EMA-binding flow cytometry assay or osmotic fragility

Folate supplementation supports haemolysis, and splenectomy reduces red cell destruction in more severe disease but raises the lifelong risk of encapsulated-organism sepsis, so vaccination and counselling are essential
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary spherocytosis results from inherited defects in proteins that anchor the red cell membrane to its underlying cytoskeleton, including spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, and protein 4.2. Weakening of these vertical linkages allows portions of the lipid bilayer to be lost, so the cell reduces its surface-area-to-volume ratio and becomes spherical rather than biconcave. These spherocytes are poorly deformable and cannot easily traverse the narrow cords of the splenic red pulp, where they are retained and prematurely destroyed by macrophages. The resulting extravascular haemolysis produces anaemia, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with jaundice, splenomegaly, and a compensatory reticulocytosis.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (spherocytes with positive direct antiglobulin test)
Other hereditary red cell membrane disorders (elliptocytosis, pyropoikilocytosis)
Clostridial or other causes of acute haemolysis
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film showing spherocytes
Bilirubin, LDH, and haptoglobin to confirm haemolysis
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune-mediated haemolysis
EMA-binding flow cytometry and/or osmotic fragility testing
Family studies and, when needed, molecular analysis of membrane protein genes
Ultrasound for gallstones and monitoring for aplastic crisis during parvovirus infection
redFlags: Aplastic crisis (often parvovirus B19) with a rapid, severe fall in haemoglobin and inappropriately low reticulocytes
Acute haemolytic crisis with worsening anaemia and jaundice
Overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis from encapsulated organisms
Symptomatic gallstone disease such as biliary obstruction or cholangitis
reference.prognosis: With supportive care and, where indicated, splenectomy, most patients have a good long-term outlook and near-normal life expectancy; the main hazards are aplastic and haemolytic crises, gallstone complications, and, after splenectomy, serious infection.
pitfalls: Mistaking hereditary spherocytosis for autoimmune haemolytic anaemia by not performing a direct antiglobulin test
Overlooking an aplastic crisis by not checking the reticulocyte count when haemoglobin drops suddenly
Forgetting folate supplementation in chronic haemolysis
Proceeding to splenectomy without appropriate vaccination and infection counselling
Missing gallstones as a cause of abdominal pain in a chronically haemolysing patient
management: Give lifelong folic acid supplementation to meet the increased demand of chronic haemolysis, with red cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia and crises

Reserve splenectomy (total or partial) for moderate-to-severe disease, preceded by vaccination against encapsulated organisms and followed by lifelong penicillin prophylaxis and prompt treatment of febrile illness
Perform cholecystectomy for symptomatic pigment gallstones, with periodic ultrasound surveillance for gallstone formation
Monitor for and urgently transfuse aplastic crisis precipitated by parvovirus B19, which abruptly suppresses erythropoiesis
Manage neonatal jaundice with phototherapy and, where severe, exchange transfusion
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given the predominantly autosomal dominant inheritance
Coordinate haematology follow-up, escalating for worsening anaemia, splenic complications or post-splenectomy sepsis
